alternative: Let the GC own memory: make release explicit (Close, context cancellation) where an external resource is involved, use runtime.AddCleanup (Go 1.24) instead of runtime.SetFinalizer for best-effort release hooks, weak.Pointer for caches that must not keep values alive, and sync.WaitGroup/atomic counters only for 'who is still using this' bookkeeping.
idiom_name: none - GC owns lifetime; explicit Close plus best-effort runtime.AddCleanup
implementation_notes: Go's runtime is a tracing collector: an embedded count can never free heap memory at zero, so the pattern's central payoff - deterministic reclamation - is unreachable and what remains is bookkeeping. What replaces the classic structure: plain references and the GC for lifetime, an explicit Close (idempotent, typically via sync.Once) for external resources, and for release hooks runtime.AddCleanup, documented as more flexible, more efficient and less error-prone than runtime.SetFinalizer (multiple cleanups per object, interior pointers, no cycle leaks, no delayed freeing) - but still best-effort, never deterministic. sync.WaitGroup or an atomic.Int32 expresses 'join on all users' when the real need is coordination rather than reference counting.
pitfalls: runtime.SetFinalizer/AddCleanup callbacks run at an unspecified time, or never for objects that live until exit; AddCleanup is documented as the better finalizer, not as deterministic release.
A count field bumped with plain ++/-- from multiple goroutines is a data race; atomic.Int32 or a mutex is required, and even then reaching zero cannot free a Go object.
A Go object cannot observe its own last reference - there is no destructor - so any release-on-last-use design must be an explicit Close protocol.
